sections.title: Part 1 · Listening to Problem Solving
sections.instructions: Listen to the conversation and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
AGENT: Thanks for calling Oakview Dental, this is Priya.
CUSTOMER: Hi, I need to cancel my appointment for tomorrow morning.
AGENT: I can help with that. Can I have your name, please?
CUSTOMER: It's Daniel Cole. My appointment is at nine fifteen.
AGENT: Found it. Is everything okay? Do you want to reschedule?
CUSTOMER: Yes, I've come down with a cold, so I don't want to come in sick.
AGENT: That's understandable. Would next Thursday at three work?
CUSTOMER: That's perfect. Thank you.
AGENT: You're welcome. I'll book that and send a confirmation email.
CUSTOMER: Great, thanks again.

From: Priya Raman <priya.raman@netmail.com>
To: reservations@lakesidehotel.com
Subject: Wrong no-show charge — booking #55107

Hello,

I booked a room for March 12 under booking #55107, but my flight was cancelled the day before due to a storm. I called your desk that same evening to cancel, and the person I spoke to said there would be no charge.

Yesterday I noticed a charge of $180 on my card for a no-show. Could you please refund it?

Thanks,
Priya Raman

From: Lakeside Hotel Reservations <reservations@lakesidehotel.com>
To: Priya Raman
Subject: Re: Wrong no-show charge — booking #55107

Hello Priya,

Thank you for writing in, and I'm sorry for the confusion. Our records show a call was received on March 11, but the cancellation was not completed in the system because of a technical error.

I have now cancelled the booking and issued a full refund of $180. Please allow three to five business days for it to appear on your statement.

As an apology, I have also added 2,000 reward points to your account.

Best regards,
Dana Cole, Reservations Manager

sections.title: Reading Part 2 · Reading to Apply a Diagram
sections.instructions: Read the instructions and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
TV wall mount installation (Model WM-30)

Parts list:
- 1 mounting plate (A)
- 2 wall brackets (B)
- 6 lag bolts (C)
- 6 washers (D)
- 1 spirit level (E)
- 1 drill template (F)

Steps:
1. Tape the drill template to the wall where you want the TV, and check it is level.
2. Drill six pilot holes through the marked spots.
3. Hold the mounting plate against the wall and insert a washer onto each lag bolt.
4. Fasten the plate to the wall using all six lag bolts.
5. Attach the two brackets to the back of the TV with the short screws (not included in the kit).
6. Lift the TV and hook the brackets onto the mounting plate, then tighten the safety screws.

sections.title: Reading Part 3 · Reading for Information
sections.instructions: Read the article and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
Habits shape far more of our lives than we realize. A habit is a behaviour that has been repeated so often it has become automatic, freeing the brain to focus on other tasks. Every habit follows a simple loop: a cue triggers a routine, and a reward reinforces it.

The cue can be a time of day, a place, or an emotion. The routine is the behaviour itself, and the reward is the satisfaction that follows. To build a new habit, experts recommend starting small. Instead of promising to exercise for an hour each day, commit to five minutes. Small wins build confidence and make the behaviour easier to repeat.

Changing your environment is also powerful. If you want to read more, leave a book on your pillow each morning. If you want to snack less, move the snacks out of sight. Making good habits convenient and bad habits inconvenient is often more effective than relying on willpower alone.

Finally, be patient. Research suggests a new habit takes anywhere from eighteen days to more than eight months to stick, depending on the person and the behaviour. The goal is progress, not perfection — missing one day does not undo the habit, but missing many in a row does.

sections.title: Reading Part 4 · Reading for Viewpoints
sections.instructions: Read the two viewpoints and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
Ban Cars Downtown: Yes
By Priya N.

Banning private cars from the downtown core would make our city healthier and safer. Fewer cars mean cleaner air, quieter streets, and fewer accidents involving pedestrians and cyclists. Cities that have introduced car-free zones have seen foot traffic and shop sales rise, not fall. With reliable buses and bike lanes, most people can still get where they need to go.

Ban Cars Downtown: No
By Tom R.

A blanket car ban ignores the people who rely on cars the most: seniors, families with young children, and delivery drivers. Many workers commute from areas with poor transit, and businesses depend on loading zones to receive goods. Instead of an outright ban, we should improve transit first and add more park-and-ride lots so driving becomes a choice rather than a necessity.
